## Analysis

**Reading the logs (speed ≈ task_score at iter 500):** C1 ≈ 7.3 m/s, C2 ≈ 6.4, C3 ≈ 5.7, C4 ≈ 5.4. C1 leads at *every* logged checkpoint; C2's slightly higher "max" (7.84) is a single unsampled-iteration blip.

**Gradient analysis at high speed (the decisive factor for iteration 3,000):**

| | d(reward)/d(v_x) at ~10 m/s |
|---|---|
| C1 | ~3.5 (clipped-linear weight 3 + raw linear 0.5 + sprint) → **pressure persists to 12–15 m/s** |
| C2 | ~0.06 (tanh saturates, surge ramp saturates at 9.5 m/s) → speed term is **flat**, so upright/heading terms dominate the gradient budget |
| C3 | ~1.0 (raw linear) but capped by height pin (0.5 m) and a mis-parsed quaternion (order assumed w,x,y,z; actual is x,y,z,w), so "upright" is really fwd_x and "body_forward" is dead (log ≈ 0) |
| C4 | ~0.22 (linear 0.2 + heavily saturated tanh) → earliest plateau of the two clean designs |

**Why C1 wins:** its reward is *dense and non-saturating in forward speed* (clipped-linear at 12 m/s + raw linear at 0.5 + sprint bonus above 5 m/s), while posture is coupled multiplicatively to speed (`upright × tanh(v_x/6)`) rather than traded off against it — the standard formulation for "as fast as possible." Its small costs (action 0.005, joint-vel 0.0005, yaw 0.02) cannot cap top speed. Only flaw is the sign-asymmetric lateral term (rewards −y drift), which costs little forward progress.

**Why C2 second:** well-designed and similarly dense early, but its speed reward saturates (tanh T=6 + ramp clip at 9.5 m/s), so late training loses speed pressure while upright (0.6·e^(...)) and heading (0.4·fwd_x) terms still pull.

**Why C4 third:** clean but weak speed gradient (0.2 linear + tanh) — it will plateau well below C1/C2; tilt-only posture shaping, no "alive" gradient beyond a constant bonus.

**Why C4-above C3:** C3's height preference (`exp(-(h-0.5)²/0.3²)`, weight 0.3) plus the quaternion-index bug corrupt the posture/speed shaping and its shaping terms saturate at ~2–3 m/s; it learned slowest of the four.
